item.title: Why Your Coping Strategy Isn't Working and What to Try
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

Why Your Coping Strategy Isn't Working and What to Try

Match your coping strategy to whether you're over- or under-activated.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Hyperarousal and hypoarousal are contrasting patterns of nervous system activation.
  • The best coping strategy depends on your nervous system's level of activation.
  • Hyperarousal requires coping strategies that decrease activation to promote feelings of safety.
  • Hypoarousal requires coping strategies that increase activation without becoming overwhelmed.

If you've ever thought, "I tried the coping strategy everyone recommends, so why do I feel worse?" you're recognizing something important. We often search for the "best" coping strategy as though there's one, best technique for everyone. But our nervous systems don't all respond to stress in the same way.

Our bodies can have different physiological stress responses. Some people feel keyed up, on edge, and irritable while others feel numb, exhausted, or disconnected. These are not signs that you're "too emotional" or "not coping well." They are often signs that your nervous system has moved outside its window of tolerance. The more useful question isn't, "What's the best coping strategy?" but, "What does my nervous system need to shift back into my window of tolerance?"

Window of Tolerance

Coined by psychiatrist Dr. Dan Siegel, the window of tolerance describes the range in which our nervous system functions best. When we are within our window of tolerance, we can feel and regulate our emotions, think clearly, solve problems, and constructively engage interpersonally.

Source: Liza Summer / Pexels

Stress can push us outside this optimal zone. When this happens, the nervous system generally moves in one of two directions: hyperarousal or hypoarousal.

These aren't discrete categories but two contrasting spectrums of nervous system activation. Hyperarousal reflects progressively increasing activation, while hypoarousal reflects progressively decreasing activation. Recognizing early signs of these shifts can help you respond before your nervous system becomes more dysregulated; thus, making it easier to return to your window of tolerance.

Hyperarousal

Hyperarousal is what many people think of when they picture anxiety. This is when your nervous system becomes activated, preparing you to fight or flee from perceived danger. You might notice:

  • Early signs: Feeling tense, restless, worried, irritable
  • Increasing activation: Racing thoughts, hypervigilance, muscle tension, rapid heartbeat, difficulty concentrating
  • Overwhelmed (Flooding): Panic, intense fear or anger, feeling emotionally overwhelmed, difficulty thinking clearly, urge to fight, flee, or escape

While all flooding involves hyperarousal, not all hyperarousal is flooding. Flooding occurs at the more extreme end of the hyperarousal spectrum. During flooding, the body’s internal alarm system signals a threat whether or not a true threat exists. Within this activated state, it becomes difficult to think clearly, listen, solve problems, or communicate effectively. As previously noted, recognizing rising activation before it reaches this extreme makes it easier to use regulation strategies while they're most effective.

Hypoarousal

Sometimes, instead of becoming more activated, the nervous system protects itself by slowing everything down. Like hyperarousal, hypoarousal exists on a spectrum. You might notice:

  • Early signs: Tired, low motivation, brain fog
  • Increasing shutdown: Emotionally numb, withdrawn, disconnected
  • Significant shutdown: Frozen, detached, dissociative shutdown

People can mistake hypoarousal for laziness or lack of motivation, when it's actually another protective survival response. Rather than experiencing too much emotional or physiological activation, a person may be experiencing too little activation to feel fully present, engaged, or able to act.

Source: AI Generated

Tailoring Strategies to Your Nervous System’s Response

There’s often an important question that gets overlooked when finding the right coping strategy for your needs: Is my nervous system overactivated or underactivated?

Coping strategies are not one-size-fits-all. Instead, the most effective coping strategies match your level and direction of activation.

Imagine two people who are both becoming dysregulated. One is pacing around the room, feeling overwhelmed, experiencing racing thoughts. The other is emotionally numb, struggling to get off the couch, feeling disconnected from everything around them.

Both of these people have been pushed outside their window of tolerance, but in opposite directions. As such, the same coping strategy for regulation likely won’t work for both people.

Once you know your direction of activation, it is easier to identify strategies to support the direction your nervous system needs to move to return to your window of tolerance.

Strategies for Hyperarousal

Source: mart production / Pexels

Your goal: Decrease activation and help your nervous system recognize that it's safe enough to slow down.

Helpful strategies include:

  • Reduce sensory stimulation, like sitting in a quiet, dimly lit room.
  • Practice paced breathing, focused on making your exhale longer than your inhale.
  • Engage in progressive muscle relaxation.
  • Break overwhelming tasks into smaller steps.
  • Limit caffeine and other stimulants.
  • Splash cold water on your face or use an ice pack on various body parts.

The goal isn't to eliminate emotion but to support slowing down your nervous system in a way that makes clear thinking and intentional action more possible.

Strategies for Hypoarousal

Your goal: Increase activation gently without becoming overwhelmed.

Helpful strategies include:

Source: Beyzaa Yurtkuran / Pexels
  • Engage in physical activity.
  • Step outside for fresh air or sunlight.
  • Use sensory stimulation, such as rubbing a textured object or smelling your favorite fragrance.
  • Practice 5-4-3-2-1 grounding.
  • Connect with a safe, trusted support person.
  • Play music that increases your energy.

The goal isn't to push yourself into overdrive. Instead, aim to gently increase activation until you can reconnect with yourself and your surroundings.

Why the Wrong Coping Strategy Can Backfire

Not every coping strategy works for every nervous system state, and when you mispair a coping strategy with an activation state, the strategy may not work in the intended way.

For example, deep breathing and meditation may feel calming when you're anxious or overstimulated (i.e., hyperaroused). But if you're already emotionally numb or disconnected (i.e., hypoaroused), focusing inward may leave you feeling even more detached.

On the other hand, listening to loud, energizing music and exercising may help someone who is feeling fatigued or shut down (i.e., hypoaroused), yet feel overstimulating to someone who is already activated (i.e., hyperaroused).

This doesn't mean these coping strategies are "good" or "bad." It means they are adaptive when matched to nervous system needs and can become maladaptive when they are not.

The Bottom Line

Your nervous system is constantly responding to cues of safety and threat. Learning to recognize the direction of these shifts can help you respond more intentionally rather than automatically. The key isn't simply having coping strategies; it's choosing ones that match whether your nervous system is under- or over-activated. So, rather than simply asking, “What's the best coping strategy?” a more helpful question is, “What strategy will help my nervous system return to my window of tolerance?”

item.title: When Helping Becomes Losing Yourself
item.description:
Self-Help

When Helping Becomes Losing Yourself

When the person everyone depends on needs help, too.

Posted August 12, 2026

I posted a photo of myself on social media and simply said, "Being a caretaker is hard." What I did not expect was the number of responses from my friends who expressed similar feelings. What also surprised me was when I looked at my own picture, I realized that I looked defeated, sad, and overly stressed. It made me realize that I needed to pay attention to myself and focus on my physical and mental health. It is a different world watching your parents age, but when they need you as a caretaker, that's when taking action to help them forces you to learn the reality of what it takes to become their helper. It's more than others' opinions of how you should feel, such as, "They took care of you as a baby," but it's facing the fact that one day, you will also lose your parents along with being their helper and that's complicated emotions.

If you are anything like me, you are a helper.

Helping others isn't simply something that we do; it becomes a part of who we are and a duty as someone who cares for people. People are complicated and we are patient with them. Patience can allow us to accept behaviors that we typically do not and people know that we will find a way to help them, but the real question is:

What happens when helpers realize that people cannot be fixed?

This is where a helper becomes uncomfortable because we may feel lost, confused, and uncertain about the person’s outcome when they do not respond as we believe is best for them. Our mental health becomes jeopardized because we focus on the why’s and how’s of their choices and behaviors to the point of exhaustion. We use our energy on others' needs before recognizing that we need help as well. Recognizing our own needs is hard. So hard that we, ourselves, maybe the hardest person to save.

When Helping Becomes Losing Yourself

We often confuse being helpful with being responsible for others’ actions, especially when you are in a helping profession. Typically, we mistake understanding someone's behavior for having to tolerate it. Helping can become part of our identity; being needed can feel purposeful, and sometimes safer than confronting our own needs. We can become so focused on solving other people's problems that we can cause ourselves physical and psychological trouble if left neglected.

Then comes the uncomfortable realization: It’s ok to be the helper and the one in need of help. You can help and also not be responsible for people, if they can still make their own choices. You cannot make someone change simply because you know what they need. We are all vulnerable to this, even when well-trained to handle complicated emotions, but that knowledge does not make us immune to our own feelings. Therefore, you can know exactly what you would advise to someone else but struggle to follow that advice when you are invested in their care.

We lose ourselves with what I coined the “Helper Mentality.” Meaning, we cannot save everyone but still strive to do so. Until we learn boundaries such as caring for others while not always saving them, we maintain this level of anxiety. Early in our helping professions, we must first learn that helping does not guarantee that a problem will be solved. As we begin to understand that we accept it and know that it doesn't mean that we give up on people. We simply recognize helping can sometimes mean telling others, “I cannot do this for you,” or simply telling them, “No” to focus on you.

Saving Yourself Isn't About Being Stronger

It's about being honest with yourself. Replace being the one who helps others with acknowledging your feelings. That's strength and it leads to inner peace. Peace will create a mindset that dictates when enough is enough for you in relation to helping others. Your level of tolerance derived from peace is strength, which allows you to keep going while questioning should you fix a problem? But, before you decide, ask yourself, “What is this costing me?”

Then, you must be ok with your answer. This question changed me professionally because I started to recognize when I was burned out and needed to prioritize my own well-being. Most importantly, I learned that I could care about others without needing to prove it. I began to say, "No" as appropriate. Before helping others, ask yourself these questions:

  • What does it cost me to keep giving when you are running on empty?
  • What does it cost me to keep showing up for someone who isn't willing to show up for themselves?
  • What does it cost me to focus on me?

“The cost” may not show up to you immediately. We can become so focused on who needs saving that we never stop asking ourselves whether or not we are the people who need saving, too. I know this because I have experienced it. Early in my career as a mental health clinician, I was so focused on my clients that I wasn't always paying attention to my needs. I became so invested in helping clients that I didn't consider what that level of giving was costing me. Then, a more seasoned clinician said something simple to me: “You need to take care of you.”

It sounds obvious, but it wasn’t, nor was it easy to change. However, I took that advice seriously. Over time, I learned how to come back to myself and maintain that mindset. I realized that caring for others does not require abandoning myself. I can care deeply about others without continually sacrificing my own well-being. In looking back to my social media post, I realized that I needed physical care (e.g., rest) in order to be well enough to help my parents.

How to Come Back to Yourself

Change your thinking and your behaviors will follow. Learn that you cannot do the work for those you are trying to help. Know that you cannot carry others’ problems or always solve them. You can extend a hand, but you cannot force them to grab it. If they do not take your hand, that does not mean you failed them either. So, stop neglecting yourself and recognize what is or not yours to carry. Put your energy toward what you can change: How you respond, what you accept, and how you take care of you.

As helpers, we will continue to care for others, but we cannot abandon our own self-care, and that's why, sometimes the person that we need to save is you.

item.title: Overthinking: When the Solution Becomes the Problem
item.description:
Anxiety

Overthinking: When the Solution Becomes the Problem

How to stop the obsessive thought loop without fighting your brain.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Problem solving moves toward an action. Looping leads toward more uncertainty.
  • Our "solutions"—overthinking, rumination, reassurance, replaying—keep the loop going in the long term.
  • Learning to allow the discomfort and stop the behaviors moves us forward

You know the feeling. Something happens—a comment lands a little off, a text goes unanswered, a thought slips in sideways. Suddenly, your brain is off to the races and the same thought keeps circling back. You think you're problem-solving, but an hour later you're no closer to an answer and feel worse than when you started.

Source: IStock/taka-hashi

What you’re experiencing is a thought loop, and if you've ever encountered one, you know it can feel impossible to break. If you have obsessive compulsive disorder, you know this cycle all too well. It may even be distressing enough to disrupt your life.

I want to help you understand why this happens, and more importantly, what you can do about it.

What Does It Mean to Be Stuck in an Obsessive Thought Loop?

Because I primarily treat people with OCD, I hear a lot about being “stuck in a thought loop.” Usually, they’re describing compulsive rumination—replaying a situation, trying to figure something out, or overthinking. They get caught in rituals, trying to relieve the distress evoked from their obsessions.

Here's an example. You're wrapping up a playdate with a friend, and you start worrying that their child was exposed to something dangerous while in your home. With each "what if," more fear, guilt, and uncertainty set in. To reassure yourself, you mentally review the entire visit: What did they touch? Were there cleaning chemicals on it? Did they put their hands in their mouth?

What you’re experiencing is an obsessive thought loop—to get rid of the feeling, you go over the thought again, hoping that this time you'll figure it out, land on something you hadn't considered, or resolve it for good so you can move on.

You might replay the afternoon, ask Google some questions, or text a friend for their take. But none of it resolves the uncertainty. The more you loop, the more anxious you feel; the more anxious you feel, the more compelled you are to keep looping.

Why Looping Thoughts Feel Like Problem-Solving (But Aren't)

Ruminating can feel productive in the moment because you’re technically doing something. But truly productive problem-solving has a beginning, middle, and end. You identify an issue, consider your options, and take action. With an obsessive loop, there's no end. The thought and feeling keep growing, pulling in more questions, what-ifs, and worst-case scenarios.

Instead of getting closer to resolution, you're feeding the loop. What makes it even harder is that stopping feels irresponsible.

Your brain argues that you'd be a bad friend (or employee, or parent, or partner) if you’d just let this go. It makes you think that you'd get clarity if only you thought about it a little more. What does it say about you if you don't try to figure it out? I mean, shouldn’t I be worried that my friend’s child may have been exposed to something toxic? Isn’t it irresponsible not to warn them that I clean with potentially toxic chemicals?

Why Looping Thoughts Are So Hard to Stop

People who struggle with looping thoughts often know, at least on some level, that the looping isn't helping. They're frustrated by it, and yet they can't stop.

Here's why.

The loop provides short-term relief from an uncomfortable feeling. Seeking reassurance, replaying events, mentally reviewing what you said or did—these behaviors temporarily reduce anxiety. But every time you loop to escape the discomfort, you're training your brain to view discomfort as intolerable, which makes it worse the next time around.

The reasons people keep looping are pretty consistent. Doing something feels better than doing nothing, even when it isn't helping. Looping might bring clarity from just one more pass through the thought. And, if the thought is distressing, not acting on it seems to suggest something bad about who you are as a person.

None of these rituals are character flaws. They make complete sense given how anxiety and OCD work. Understanding them is the first step toward changing them.

How to Break an Obsessive Thought Loop

Breaking the loop isn’t about stopping the thoughts or making them go away. Trying to suppress a thought is like being told not to think about a pink elephant—your brain immediately goes there.

In the playdate example, the goal would be to stop the mental behaviors that keep the thoughts looping. You learn how to keep moving forward anyway, without seeking reassurance, replaying the afternoon, or looping. That uncertainty doesn't have to be resolved for you to live your life.

Here are some simple (though not always easy) steps to get you started:

1. Notice that you're in the loop.

This sounds obvious, I know, but many people are so deep in the loop that they don't realize they're looping. They think they're just thinking. There is a difference, and awareness is the start of change.

2. Refocus your attention outside your own head.

What's around you right now? What can you see, hear, or touch? Pull your attention from the internal spiral back to the present moment and the life that's actually happening in front of you.

3. Expect to feel uncomfortable when you stop.

This is the part most people miss. When you interrupt the loop without resolving it, the anxiety doesn't immediately disappear. In fact, it often gets louder first. That's okay. That discomfort is the point—learning to tolerate it without running back to the loop is exactly how you build the capacity to break the pattern for good. The looping makes the situation worse by intensifying and prolonging the doubt.

The goal is to get some time and distance from the situation before drawing conclusions. These thoughts can feel urgent in the moment. With a little space—an hour, a day—you'll often find they were neither as important nor as catastrophic as they initially seemed.

item.title: What Sam Altman Wouldn’t Ask ChatGPT
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

What Sam Altman Wouldn’t Ask ChatGPT

What Harvard, a spiritual teacher, and your vagus nerve know about AI limits.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Happiness comes from relationships, not achievement or information.
  • Breathwork and meditation help reduce stress and rewire the brain for peace.
  • AI can explain happiness, but it cannot truly experience or cultivate it.

When OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was asked what he would never turn to ChatGPT for, his answer seemed to me to be disarmingly honest: "I think I would never ask it, like, how to be happy. I would rather ask a wise person." That's a remarkable admission from the man who helped build what is among the world's most powerful AI chatbots.

And yet, I did exactly what he advised against—I asked ChatGPT how to be happy. The response was thoughtful, well-organized, and, in a certain way, correct. It listed the usual suspects: cultivate relationships, practice gratitude, exercise, sleep, find meaning, limit social media. If you were looking for a tidy summary of the scientific literature, it delivered.

The Limits of AI and Happiness

Which raises the real question: Why can't AI tell us how to be happy? The blunt answer is that ChatGPT has no emotions, no lived experience, and no stake in whether you wake up tomorrow feeling joy or despair. It can synthesize vast libraries of psychology research and perhaps produce a competent listicle.

But happiness is not an information problem; it is an experiential one. One of the people responsible for ChatGPT essentially acknowledged that some human questions require a human—or at least something that has felt something. A large language model can describe happiness the way a travel guidebook describes Paris. Neither has ever actually been there.

The World Is Not Getting Happier

Before we talk about how to become happy, it's worth asking: How happy are we, actually?

This conversation matters because the data tells a worrying story. The United States ranked 23rd in the 2026 World Happiness Report, its lowest-ever ranking, with young adults faring particularly poorly. Globally, happiness indices have plateaued or declined across many high-income nations, even as material prosperity has grown. If information and abundance were enough to make us happy, we would already be the happiest civilization in history. Clearly, something else is at work.

What Actually Makes People Happy—Or Unhappy?

Science has a fairly consistent answer, and it has little to do with achievement or optimization. The Harvard Study of Adult Development, one of the longest-running studies of human flourishing, now spanning nearly 80 years, found that close relationships, more than money, fame, or even genes, are the single strongest predictor of happiness and longevity. Its lead researchers concluded: "The key to healthy aging is relationships."

Following Sam Altman’s advice to seek wisdom from a wise person, I turned to someone I consider a wise person: Gurudev Sri Sri Ravi Shankar, a spiritual guide and founder of the Art of Living Foundation. His perspective adds another dimension: Happiness is not something you acquire from outside but something you uncover within. "Deep inside you is a fountain of bliss, a fountain of joy," he said. "There is no guilt there. There is no fear there." He also reminded me, pointedly: "If you are a taker of happiness you get misery; if you are a giver of happiness you get joy and love."

Rather than chasing happiness directly, consider flipping the question: What makes us unhappy? This is, in essence, the approach of yogic philosophy—remove the obstacles, and what remains is your natural state of equanimity. Think about the small daily triggers: A colleague doesn't send a critical document, and your morning unravels. Someone blames you for something you didn't do, and your mind churns on it for hours. These are not tragedies, yet they can hijack our peace entirely. If we can identify and gradually neutralize these micro-disturbances, we stop leaking happiness. What's left over doesn't need to be manufactured; it simply is.

Meditation: Rewiring the Brain for Happiness

If happiness is a practice, and stress is its primary obstacle, meditation is arguably one of the most evidence-based tools we have. Meditation produces measurable, lasting physiological changes. Research shows that regular practice reduces cortisol—the body's primary stress hormone—alongside structural changes in brain regions governing emotional regulation. Meditation doesn't just shift your mood; it physically restructures the brain that generates “unhappiness.”

Not everyone can sit still. Fortunately, there is an even simpler entry point: breathwork. The vagus nerve—the tenth cranial nerve—is the main highway of the parasympathetic ("rest and digest") nervous system. Controlled, deliberate breathing directly stimulates it. Pranayama-style breathing at roughly 6 breaths per minute synchronizes cardiorespiratory rhythms at the resonant frequency, enhancing vagal tone and baroreflex sensitivity (Lehrer and Gevirtz).

One particular rhythmic breathwork practice—Sudarshan Kriya Yoga (SKY)—has been studied in different populations. A Stanford University study showed that SKY was able to normalize veterans’ anxiety in one week, with benefits that persisted at one year. A recent randomized trial in JAMA Network Open found that SKY significantly reduced stress, anxiety, depression, and burnout among physicians.

You can breathe anywhere. You do not need an app. You do not need ChatGPT.

So Where Does That Leave AI?

ChatGPT is extraordinary at information. In my view, if you don't know what gratitude journaling is, or what the Harvard Study of Adult Development found, or what controlled breathing does—ask away. Generative AI can be a fine tutor.

But happiness is not a fact to retrieve. It is a state to cultivate every day, in small moments: when someone blames you unfairly, when the email doesn't arrive, when the mind begins to churn. In those moments, one of the best tools that can help is the one you have already practiced: a breath, a meditation, a call to someone you love, a deliberate refusal to hand over your peace of mind.

Sam Altman was right to ask a wise man. Better yet, become one.

Disclosure: Dr. Chhatwal has practiced meditation and breathwork techniques, including SKY (Sudarshan Kriya Yoga), for over 20 years and volunteers as a teacher of these techniques with the Art of Living Foundation. He has no financial relationship or official affiliation with the foundation.

item.title: Postpartum Psychosis: A Clinical Perspective on a Tragic Case
item.description:
Postpartum Psychosis

Postpartum Psychosis: A Clinical Perspective on a Tragic Case

Postpartum psychosis may initially resemble anxiety or depression.

Posted August 12, 2026

The Lindsay Clancy murder trial has captured national attention. When a mother in suburban Duxbury, Massachusetts, seemingly picture-perfect with three young children, strangles her children (ages 8 months, 3, and 5), the question arises: Could this happen to anyone, anywhere?

As a reproductive psychiatrist with over two decades of experience, I have treated more than a thousand women with postpartum depression and anxiety, and fewer than twenty with postpartum psychosis. The condition is rare, occurring in 1–2 per 1,000 postpartum women, but devastating. Postpartum psychosis typically presents with fluctuating symptoms: mood disturbance (depression, elevated or irritable mood), psychotic features (delusions, hallucinations, illogical thoughts), and sometimes bizarre behavior. In most cases, it represents a bipolar-spectrum mood disorder rather than a primary psychotic illness.

The Challenge of Recognition

In my clinical practice, I have encountered subtle presentations of postpartum psychosis. Women may appear sad, depressed, anxious, or agitated, often with severe sleep disturbance. When sleep deprivation persists and antidepressants fail to help, symptoms can worsen. In a subset of women with underlying postpartum psychosis, antidepressants may actually exacerbate the presentation, triggering irritability, agitation, and worsening insomnia.

Patients frequently use socially acceptable language: "I’m so anxious," "I’m exhausted." They rarely volunteer paranoid ideation or auditory hallucinations. Intrusive thoughts about wanting to die, or distressing images of harm to the baby, can occur in both postpartum psychosis and postpartum OCD. Distinguishing whether a postpartum woman with intrusive thoughts is at risk for harming herself or her infant is one of the most challenging aspects of our work. Clinical textbooks suggest that if a woman has no intent to act on suicidal or frightening thoughts, she more likely has postpartum OCD. However, the reality in clinical practice is that postpartum psychosis can wax and wane; a woman may appear stable for part of the day, then experience a surge of symptoms.

My colleagues and I, with over sixty years of collective experience, regularly present challenging cases in peer supervision. We review postpartum depression, postpartum OCD, and occasionally postpartum psychosis to ensure we are not "missing something" and to discuss the most effective treatments for complicated patients.

The Lindsay Clancy Case: A Familiar Presentation

Lindsay Clancy reported symptoms consistent with postpartum anxiety: stress, anxiety, difficulty sleeping, feeling overwhelmed at the prospect of returning to work as a labor and delivery nurse and leaving her young children. I have treated countless postpartum women with similar complaints. The differential diagnosis is broad: postpartum depression, postpartum OCD, postpartum psychosis, and postpartum PTSD.

Telehealth has become standard in mental health care. Many clinicians gave up office space during the pandemic and moved fully virtual. In my practice, approximately 20% of patients see me in person; the majority prefer telehealth. For clinical reasons, I request in-person visits when puzzled by a presentation. Office appointments can reveal information that telehealth cannot capture—a paranoid patient might hesitate to disclose concerns that her apartment is bugged by the CIA through a screen, but might open up about psychotic symptoms in person.

Medicine, Law, and Language

Our legal system operates in black and white, good versus evil, while medicine, and psychiatry specifically, focuses on symptoms, treatments, and treatment response. We speak different languages. We live in a litigious society: when tragedy strikes, lawyers are hired, courts convene, and the goal becomes holding someone responsible. In this case, Lindsay Clancy's attorney has focused on psychiatric medications as one culprit, and the prescribers as another. The attorney repeatedly refers to SSRIs as "strong chemicals that change the brain." He has also emphasized her outpatient psychiatrist's limited experience, noting she had graduated from residency only months before joining a group practice and beginning telehealth treatment with Clancy.

Raising Awareness

The Lindsay Clancy murder trial is raising awareness of perinatal mental illness. News outlets are interviewing experts to differentiate postpartum depression from postpartum psychosis. Hopefully, this will lead family members, friends, and physicians to consider postpartum psychosis on their differential when a loved one or patient reports severe symptoms unresponsive to "usual treatments" for postpartum depression or anxiety.

Greater awareness should lead to more women receiving appropriate treatment. Postpartum Support International, a nonprofit organization, offers free virtual support groups for pregnant and postpartum women in the United States. PSI also has regional coordinators worldwide who help connect pregnant and postpartum women to clinicians specializing in women's mental health. Additionally, PSI has a team of reproductive psychiatrists who provide expert consultation to attorneys representing women with legal issues related to perinatal mental health conditions.

A "Bad Disease"

My husband is an oncologist. Throughout his training and career, he often referred to certain cancer diagnoses as "bad disease," an informal term used when standard treatments were insufficient to prevent progression and death. In reproductive psychiatry, postpartum psychosis is a "bad disease." It can masquerade as anxiety or depression, worsen with "usual treatments," and ultimately carries risk of suicide and infanticide.

Lindsay Clancy's clinical course, worsening symptoms over several months, two emergency department visits, an evaluation at a specialized women's mental health day hospital program, and an inpatient admission to McLean Hospital, suggests that the "usual treatments" were insufficient to stabilize her.

Would a longer inpatient stay at McLean have made a difference? Would consistent engagement with the Women & Infants day hospital program have changed the outcome? If Lindsay Clancy had consistently taken her prescribed psychiatric medications, would her three children be alive today? These questions are unanswerable.

Regardless of the legal outcome, the tragic deaths of Cora, Callen, and Dawson will profoundly affect everyone who knew the Clancy family and all who have followed this case for years to come.
